[Climate change] Present-day climate change includes both global warming—the ongoing increase in global average temperature—and its wider effects on Earth's climate system. In a broader sense, climate change also includes previous long-term changes to Earth's climate. The modern-day rise in global temperatures is driven by human activities, especially fossil fuel (coal, oil and natural gas) burning since the Industrial Revolution. Fossil fuel use, deforestation, and some agricultural and industrial practices release greenhouse gases. These gases absorb some of the heat that the Earth radiates after it warms from sunlight, warming the lower atmosphere. Earth's atmosphere now has roughly 50% more carbon dioxide, the main gas driving global warming, than it did at the end of the pre-industrial era, reaching levels not seen for millions of years. Climate change has an increasingly large impact on the environment. Heat waves and wildfires are becoming more common. Amplified warming in the Arctic has contributed to thawing permafrost, retreat of glaciers and sea ice decline. Higher temperatures are also causing more intense storms, droughts, and other weather extremes. Rapid environmental change in mountains, coral reefs, and the Arctic is forcing many species to relocate or become extinct. Even if efforts to minimize future warming are successful, some effects will continue for centuries. These include ocean heating, ocean acidification and sea level rise. Climate change threatens people with increased flooding, extreme heat, increased food and water scarcity, more disease, and economic loss. Human migration and conflict can also be a result. The World Health Organization calls climate change one of the biggest threats to global health in the 21st century. Societies and ecosystems will experience more severe risks without action to limit warming. 21 October: the Emissions Gap Report 2026 said that, to minimize peak warming and return to 1.5 °C by 2100, to achieve a 'lowest possible' 1.5 °C overshoot scenario in which peak warming is limited to 1.7–1.8 °C by mid-century, greenhouse gas emissions would have to be cut by 18% by 2030, 45% by 2035 and 69% by 2040, all relative to 2025 levels.
10 September: a study published in Environmental Research Letters estimated that warming-induced emissions (WIE) of greenhouse gases from natural sources (permafrost, wetlands, freshwaters, wildfire)—which are not represented by most current climate models—could add 0.2 °C–0.4  °C of global warming by 2100.
30 September: a study published in Nature Geoscience that constrained ice-sheet model projections with satellite observations concluded that the Antarctic ice sheet is very likely (≥92% probability) to lose mass overall by 2100 even under aggressive emissions-reduction scenarios, and that higher emissions very likely increase this loss.
12 October: a study published in Nature Communications estimated that the global mean sea level could rise 30±6 millimeters (1.18±0.24 inches) by 2100 due to melting of Thwaites Glacier, approximately doubling prior projections even if no further climate warming takes place.
The estimated additional warming by 2100 due to warming-induced emissions is 0.2 °C to 0.4 °C. FINAL: 0.2 °C to 0.4 °C.
